Title: Porous Nanoframe Based Plasmonic Structure With High‐Density Hotspots for the Quantitative Detection of Gaseous Benzaldehyde

Porous Nanoframe Based Plasmonic Structure With
High-Density Hotspots for the Quantitative Detection of
Gaseous Benzaldehyde
Guoqiang Fang, Xiang Lin,* Jinlei Wu, Wen Xu, Wuliji Hasi,* and Bin Dong*
Owing to its high sensitivity, surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) has
immense potential for the identiﬁcation of lung cancer from the variation in
volatile biomarkers in the exhaled gas. However, two prevailing factors limit
the application of SERS: 1) the adsorption of target molecules into SERS
hotspots and 2) the detection speciﬁcity in multiple interference
environments. To improve the density of the SERS hotspots, 3D Au@Ag-Au
particles are prepared in a porous nanoframes (PPFs) based plasmonic
structure, which facilitated a richer local electromagnetic ﬁeld distribution
among the Au nanocubic (NC) cores, Au-Ag porous nanoframes, and Au
nanoparticles, thereby promoting the adsorption probability of gaseous
aldehydes into the hotspots. L-cysteines (l-Cys)-modiﬁed 3D Au@Ag-Au PPFs
are proposed as a benzaldehyde (BA) gas detection carrier to accurately detect
biomarkers in complex exhaled gases and eliminate interference from other
components. Unlike the conventional use of 4-aminothiophenol as a linker
molecule, the novel L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS substrate is sensitive toward the
aldehyde molecules and immune to other volatile organic compounds
(ethanol, cyclohexane, toluene, etc.). Furthermore, a medical mask consisting
of this SERS substrate is designed to realize intelligent detection of gaseous
BA concentrations assisted by a machine learning algorithm.

1. Introduction
Primary bronchial lung cancer, commonly
referred to as lung cancer, which originates
in the bronchial mucosa or glands, and is
regarded as one of the most prevalent ma-
lignancies worldwide.[1] As the initial stage
of lung cancer does not signiﬁcantly aﬀect
patient health, most patients tend to ignore
the disease and lose the best opportunity for
clinical treatment. Consequently, lung can-
cer has the highest mortality rate among
all malignant tumors. Early diagnosis and
timely cure of lung cancer can considerably
reduce mortality rates.[2] Currently, low-
dose computed tomography of the chest
is an accurate and eﬃcient technique for
screening early lung cancer lesions. How-
ever, low -dose computed tomography re-
quires specialized equipment and experi-
enced practitioners for its operation and
interpretation.[3] Therefore, low-risk and in-
telligent diagnostic tools to identify lung
cancer at an early stage are required.
Gaseous aldehydes in exhaled human
breath have been reported to be typi-
cal biomarkers for early lung malignan-
cies and have enormous potential for early
assisted screening and diagnosis of lung cancer.[4–9] Surface-
enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is a powerful spectral anal-
ysis technique used for capturing gas molecules and provid-
ing ﬁngerprint signals.[10–17] The most important advantage of
SERS is that it is nondestructive, fast, and free from water in-
terference, rendering it ideal for clinical diagnosis.[18–25] How-
ever, most gaseous aldehydes produce weak-intensity signals in
their Raman spectra because of their low Raman scattering cross-
section.4 In addition, gaseous molecules diﬀuse faster than liquid
molecules owing to the greater free space.[26,27] The high diﬀu-
sion rate results in inadequate contact between the gaseous alde-
hydes and the SERS substrate, thus reducing the probability of
their adsorption onto the substrate. Consequently, gaseous alde-
hydes cannot be directly detected using SERS substrates in most
cases.
In this regard, metal‒organic framework (MOF) structures
with high porosities and large speciﬁc surface areas have
attracted considerable attention.[27,28] Although MOF-coated
nanoparticles (NPs) have achieved promising results in the ﬁeld

of gas detection, the MOF structure also hinders the localized
surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) eﬀect between adjacent metal
NPs, which reduces the detection sensitivity for gaseous alde-
hydes. In addition, highly sensitive SERS substrates modiﬁed
with special functional groups are eﬀective for detecting gaseous
aldehydes. Typically, 4-aminothiophenol (4-ATP) molecules are
employed as bridges for connecting SERS substrates to gaseous
aldehydes.[8,29–31] The sulfhydryl-containing end is connected to
the SERS substrate in the form of an Au–S or Ag–S bond,
while the exposed amino group at the other end undergoes
a Schiﬀbase reaction with aldehydes, resulting in a detection
limit as low as 10 ppb for 4-ethylbenzaldehyde (EBA). However,
the 4-ATP molecules are susceptible to volatile organic com-
pounds that are not gas markers of lung cancer. More impor-
tantly, they are susceptible to coupling reactions forming 4,4′-
dimercaptoazobenzene upon laser irradiation, and the dynamic
Raman characteristic peaks inevitably increase the diﬃculty of
quantifying trace aldehyde concentrations.[32]
In this study, we designed and prepared 3D Au@Ag-Au par-
ticles in a porous nanoframe (PPF) plasmonic structure consist-
ing of an Au nanocubic (NC) core and Ag-Au porous nanoframes
(PFs) embedded with small Au NPs (Figure 1). The PPFs struc-
ture is conducive to a richer pattern of local electric ﬁeld distribu-
tion between the Au NC core, Au-Ag PFs, and Au NPs, leading to
detection limits that are two orders of magnitude lower for the 4-
mercaptobenzoic acid (4-MBA) molecules than for the traditional
Au NCs. The Au@Ag-Au PPFs SERS substrate was functionally
modiﬁed with L-cysteine (L-Cys) to eﬃciently capture aldehyde
molecules via an acylation reaction. The L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS
substrate was sensitive to the recognition of aldehyde molecules
(benzaldehyde (BA), EBA, etc.) and independent of other volatile
organic compounds (ethanol, cyclohexane, toluene, etc.). Finally,
the highly sensitive SERS detection of BA combined with an
advanced convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm model
completes automated data analysis to achieve accurate BA con-
centration prediction.
2. Result and Discussion
Rational design of metal NP morphology is particularly im-
portant for applications based on the LSPR eﬀect.[33–37] In
SERS, the Raman signals are highly ampliﬁed at the so-called
hotspots, which are regions with extremely strong electromag-
netic ﬁelds.[38,39] In addition to the generation of sharp tips and
rough surfaces via morphology-controlled synthesis, hotspots
can also be constructed by creating nanogaps on or within
metallic nanostructures.[22,31,40–42] Notably, 3D metal nanomate-
rials comprising multiple hotspot types exhibit excellent SERS
performance.[34,43] Therefore, we designed and prepared a porous
Au@Ag-Au PPFs structure with built-in nanogaps and rough-
ened surfaces to integrate the lightning rod eﬀect and intraparti-
cle coupling eﬀect into a single entity.

The fabrication of Au@Ag-Au PPFs involved three major
steps, as illustrated schematically in Figure 1. First, the Au NCs
were prepared using the seed growth method (Step 1).[34] Au@Ag
NCs were then prepared by depositing Ag atoms on the Au NCs
via chemical reduction (Step 2).[44] Finally, the galvanic replace-
ment reaction occurred between the Ag shell and AuCl3
−leading
to the etching of Ag atoms from the side faces of the Au@Ag
NCs. The mixture of ascorbic acid (AA) and NaOH accelerated
the reduction of Ag+ and AuCl3
−, resulting in the co-deposition
of Au and Ag atoms on the edges and corners of the Ag shell, thus
forming Au@Ag-Au PFs (Step 3).[45] Upon further increasing the
concentration of NaOH and AuCl3
−in the precursor solution,
most of the Au+ was independently reduced to Au nanospheres
in the solution, while some of the Au+ was reduced to NPs on
the surface of the Au@Ag-Au PFs, forming Au@Ag-Au dots in
the porous-nanoframes (DPFs) structure. The Au@Ag-Au PPFs
(with more Au particles in the nanoframe) were formed with in-
creasing NaOH and AuCl3
−concentrations.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning elec-
tron microscopy (SEM) were used to monitor the structural evo-
lution during the synthesis of Au@Ag-Au PPFs. Figure 2A–E
demonstrates the structure and model schematics of the NPs
during the synthesis process. High uniformity in the sizes and
shapes was clearly observed in the SEM morphological images of
the NPs, indicating a controllable and mature synthesis method.
The SEM image of the Au@Ag-Au PPFs shows that the struc-
ture is open on the {100} facets and has a large number of Au
NPs embedded in the Au-Ag nano-frame (Figure 2E). Moreover,
we supplemented our ﬁndings with high-magniﬁcation TEM im-
ages to verify the formation of Au NPs on the Ag nano-shell sur-
faces (Figure S1, Supporting Information). Energy dispersive
Spectroscopy (EDS) images characterizing the elemental map-
ping showed that the proportions of Au and Ag atoms in the PPFs
structure were 10 and 90% (Figure 2F,G), respectively, which
were derived from the elemental ratio of Au to Ag at 15 nm.
Each NP formed during the morphological evolution was an-
alyzed via ultraviolet‒visible‒near infrared (UV‒Vis‒NIR) spec-
troscopy, as shown in Figure 2H. The extinction spectrum of the
Au NCs exhibited a resonance peak at 545 nm. The extinction
spectrum of the Au@Ag NCs showed three peaks, and the main
resonance peak (509 nm) was blue-shifted owing to the reduc-
tion of the Ag ions on the surface of the Au NCs. The absorption
peak at 342 nm was primarily attributed to the LSPR eﬀect on
the Au@Ag cubic {100} facets. The absorption peaks at 394 and
509 nm were observed owing to the dipole generated by split-
ting of the dipole formants at the sharp corners of the Au@Ag
NCs.[46] As the galvanic replacement reaction proceeded, the in-
tensity of the plasmonic extinction band corresponding to the Ag
cube gradually decreased, and the resonance peaks observed in
the higher-wavelength region gradually redshifted. Moreover, the
coupling between the Au NPs and Ag nano-shell led to the broad-
ening of the absorption peak and a redshift of the SPR peak (from
PFs to DPFs). As the amount of Au NPs on the Ag nano-shell sur-
face increased, the SPR peak position continued to redshift, and
the full width at half maximum continued to broaden.
To gain further insights into the optical properties of the plas-
monic Au@Ag-Au PPFs, ﬁnite-diﬀerence time-domain (FDTD)
simulations were performed to simulate the extinction, absorp-
tion, and scattering spectra (Figure 2I). The directions of the in-
cident light and polarization are shown in the inset image. The
simulation results deviated slightly from the experimental results
because of the complexity of the structure and composition of
the plasmonic Au@Ag-Au PPFs. However, the main peak located
at 583 nm matched well with the experimentally obtained reso-
nance peak at 558 nm. The 785 nm portable Raman spectrometer
was used for the spectral acquisition, in which the electromag-
netic near-ﬁeld of the Au@Ag-Au PPFs was simulated under the
785 nm laser excitation at diﬀerent polarized incidences (x- and
y-axes).
The oscillating electric ﬁeld along the x- and y-axes produced
a strong hotspot at the tip of the NP with a calculated maximum
|E|/E0 (EMax) of 35.24 and 34.16, respectively (Figure S2, Support-
ing Information). The average value of the electric ﬁeld (EAve) in
the cube at 2 nm away from the NPs was calculated to visualize
the quality of the hotspots. The results of the electric ﬁeld distri-
bution for the four types of NPs are shown in Figure S3 (Support-
ing Information). A single Au@Ag-Au PPFs structure generated
enriched electric ﬁeld distribution patterns. The maximum and
average electric ﬁeld strengths were 8.69 and 2.53 times higher
than those of the Au@Ag NCs, respectively.
To build bulk substrates with the resulting NPs, closely packed
NP monolayers were prepared using an interfacial assembly
method.[47,48] As shown in Figure 3A, the assembled Au@Ag-Au
PPF array exhibited multiple hotspots at the corners and bumps
and intraparticle and interparticle gaps, resulting in strong elec-
tromagnetic near-ﬁeld focusing.[49–51] The SEM images of the
NPs monolayers on the silicon wafer are shown in Figure 3B–F.
This interfacial self-assembly technique allows the formation of
a densely packed monolayer of NPs over a large area with excel-
lent uniformity. Considering that hotspots are mainly generated
with gaps between the neighboring NPs, we determined the par-
ticle density of the NPs and the coverage of the SERS substrates,
which indirectly reﬂects the number of hotspots. The optical pho-
tographs, particle density (256 counts um−2), and coverage of
the SERS substrate (92.16%) for the Au@Ag-Au PPFs revealed
a high density of hotspot distribution in the SERS substrate of
the Au@Ag-Au PPFs (Figure S4, Supporting Information).
A simulation model of the NP arrays was established based
on the locally enlarged SEM images, and the electric ﬁeld distri-
bution of the NPs arrays at the excitation wavelength of 785 nm
was simulated (Figure 3G–K). The electromagnetic enhancement
of the Au NCs and Au@Ag NCs arrays primarily occurred in
the gaps between the neighboring NPs. This agrees well with
the strong ﬁeld enhancement observed for the plasmonic dimer.
The Au@Ag-Au PFs, Au@Ag-Au DPFs, and Au@Ag-Au PPFs ar-
rays also exhibited a large number of built-in hotspots owing to
their unique hollow structures. In contrast, the enhancement of
hotspots between the Au NPs in the gaps was higher than that
in the plane gaps. To further demonstrate the near-ﬁeld focusing
ability of the plasmonic Au@Ag-Au PPFs, we performed SERS
measurements using 4-MBA as a model Raman probe. The SERS
substrates were incubated in a solution containing 4-MBA, and
the SERS spectra were obtained under excitation with the 785 nm
laser (Figure 3L–P and Figure S5, Supporting Information). The
limit of detection (LOD) of the Au@Ag-Au PPFs for 4-MBA was
10−10 m, which was signiﬁcantly higher than that of the Au NCs.
The SERS intensity from the Au@Ag NCs to Au@Ag-Au PPFs
continued to increase as the replacement reaction proceeded,

used for Au@Ag-Au PPFs, Au NSs@Ag NCs and Au CNCs@Ag
NCs were prepared using positive-curvature gold nano-spheres
(NSs) and negative-curvature Au concave nano-cubes (CNC) as
cores. Subsequently, Au NSs@Ag-Au PPFs and Au CNCs@Ag-
Au PPFs were prepared by the same replacement reduction re-
action. The SEM and TEM images of the as-prepared NPs are
shown in Figure 4A–D and E–H. The morphology of the NPs
prepared in each step was uniform, and the structure was well-
deﬁned. The extinction spectra of each type of NPs were recorded
using UV–Vis–NIR spectroscopy, as shown in Figure 4I–K and L–
N. Interestingly, the pattern of the resonance peak changes dur-
ing morphological evolution was consistent and independent of
the Au core. 4-MBA (10−6 m) was used to investigate the SERS

Lung cancer is a malignant tumor with the highest incidence
rate. Therefore, it is important to develop a rapid and accurate
early diagnostic method to reduce the mortality rate of lung can-
cer patients. The average concentrations of major volatile organic
compounds (ketones) present in the exhaled air of cancer pa-
tients are signiﬁcantly higher than those in healthy individuals.
Moreover, octanal, BA, heptanal, and EBA were not found in the
exhaled air of healthy volunteers.[28,52–54] However, the small Ra-
man scattering cross section renders it diﬃcult for the SERS tech-
nique to directly detect the characteristic C═O chemical bonds.
Conventional solid substrates are unsuitable for carrying and col-
lecting gas. Therefore, we developed an L-Cys-modiﬁed Au@Ag-
Au PPFs SERS sensor to eﬀectively capture gaseous BA. The 3D
morphology of and open internal spaces in the Au@Ag-Au PPFs
allowed eﬃcient transport of analytes, leading to an increased
probability of detecting low concentrations of molecules in the
gas phase.[31] The ─SH group of the L-Cys molecule was attached
to the surface of the NPs, and the exposed ─NH2 group at the
other end underwent a Schiﬀbase reaction with the ─CHO group
(Figure 5A).
Because there are no reports on the use of L-Cys-modiﬁed
SERS substrates for trapping aldehyde molecules, we ﬁrst at-
tempted to incubate the L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS substrate in a so-
lution containing BA (10−2 m) for 30 min. The disappearance of
the SH vibrational peak (at 2554 cm−1) in the L-Cys SERS spectra
conﬁrmed the adsorption of L-Cys onto the Au@Ag-Au PPFs via
the sulfur atoms after S–H bond breakage (Figure S6, Supporting
Information). As shown in Figure 5B, the Raman spectra of L-Cys
+ BA exhibited characteristic peaks at 835 and 1001 cm−1, which
may be attributed to the C═N stretching vibration of the reaction
product of L-Cys and BA.[15] The peak at 1597 cm−1 corresponds
to the cyclic C-C in-plane bending. The shift in the peak at 1135
cm−1 may be due to a change in the C-S stretching pattern of the
reaction products of L-Cys and BA.

Notably, 4-ATP-modiﬁed SERS substrates are widely used to
detect aldehyde gases. Therefore, the performances of the 4-ATP-
modiﬁed and L-Cys-modiﬁed Au@Ag-Au PPFs
SERS substrates were individually investigated (Figure 5C). In
terms of stability, the characteristic Raman peak positions of BA
on the L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS substrate remained constant with
increasing laser power (Figure 5D). When the laser power ex-
ceeded 90 mW, the L-Cys molecules were damaged and the in-
tensity of the characteristic peaks decreased (Figure S7, Support-
ing Information). However, 4-ATP on the surface of the metal
NPs was prone to oxidative coupling with oxygen under laser ir-
radiation (Figure S8, Supporting Information). The relative in-
tensities of the characteristic Raman peaks of BA on the 4-ATP-
modiﬁed SERS substrate changed with increasing laser power
(Figure 5E). The SERS spectra of octanal, formaldehyde, hep-
taldehyde, BA, EBA, and acetone on the L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS
substrate are shown in Figure S9 (Supporting Information). Sig-
niﬁcant diﬀerences were observed between the SERS spectra of
BA and EBA. The SERS substrate was insensitive to acetone, oc-
tanal, formaldehyde, and heptaldehyde. In contrast, the 4-ATP-
modiﬁed SERS substrate can be used for the sensitive detec-
tion of octanal, BA, EBA, and acetone; however, their Raman
peaks overlap with the characteristic Raman peaks of the 4-ATP
molecule, which is very unfavorable for the trace analysis of sub-
stances (Figure S10, Supporting Information).[32,55,56]
Furthermore, other volatile organic molecules such as ethanol
(EtOH), n-hexane, n-butanol, n-pentyl, methanol, and toluene
(10−2 m) were used to evaluate the speciﬁcity of the SERS sen-
sor. Figure 5F displays the Raman spectra of the L-Cys-modiﬁed

and after the adsorption of organic molecules by this SERS sen-
sor, we introduced the concept of spectral angle to quantify the
diﬀerence in the spectra (Figure 5G). For details on the spectral
angle, please refer to Supporting Information. A higher similar-

signiﬁcant speciﬁcity for BA and EBA and was independent of the
interference of alkanes, aromatic hydrocarbons, or alcohols. Be-
cause the SERS spectrum of EBA is signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from
that of BA, the L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS sensors could detect BA in
the presence of other aldehydes. Therefore, L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS
substrates exhibited a higher potential for gaseous aldehyde de-
tection and analysis.
For proof-of-concept, we designed a mask-type SERS chip
combined with a machine learning algorithm (Figure 6A) to real-
ize the automated detection of BA concentration in exhaled gas.
In brief, 3D ﬁlter paper-based SERS substrates were prepared by
assembling the Au@Ag-Au PPFs on a ﬁlter paper (Figure S11,
Supporting Information). The preparation process of the large-
area ﬁlter paper-based SERS substrate has been previously re-
ported by our group.[34] The mask sensor for BA detection in ex-
haled gas was prepared by sandwiching an L-Cys-modiﬁed SERS
sensor in a medical face mask. Considering the permeability of
the ﬁlter paper sensor, this not only facilitates portability but also
helps the adsorption of exhaled aldehyde gases. Spectra were then
recorded for the SERS sensor, which was removed after wearing
the mask sensor for a certain period. The spectra were input into
a CNN algorithm for an accurate and automated concentration
recognition. Finally, the health assessment information of the pa-
tient was derived based on the BA concentration, and the results
were presented in the form of a quick response code. Although
this substrate was developed for potential applications in the case
of patients with lung cancer, it has not been tested for real pa-
tients.
Typically, aldehydes (analytes) exist in a liquid state. In this
study, we heated the BA solution to the boiling point in a closed
container to obtain gaseous BA and veriﬁed the ability of the
SERS sensor to detect gaseous BA. Please refer to Supporting
Information for details regarding the conversion of liquid BA
to gaseous BA.[8] Figure 6B shows the Raman spectra of the
SERS sensor after reaction with diﬀerent concentrations of BA.

BA was successfully detected at concentrations as low as 1 ppb.
Raman spectra of 100 points were collected over an area of 500
× 500 μm2 (Figure 6C) to further evaluate the homogeneity of
this SERS sensor. The average relative standard deviation (RSD)
within this area was 11.68%, indicating that the performance of
the Au@Ag-Au PPF SERS substrate was highly uniform. In ad-
dition, Au@Ag-Au PPFs SERS substrates prepared from 10 dif-
ferent batches exhibited similar SERS performances with a coef-
ﬁcient of variation of less than 10% (Figure 6D). Because sens-
ing relies on chemical adsorption and the reaction processes be-
tween gaseous BA and the sensor, the adsorption time must be
longer than 30 min to obtain the best detection performance
(Figure 6E and Figure S12, Supporting Information). Because
the stability of the SERS substrates in air is also an important
parameter, the temporal stability of the Au@Ag-Au PPFs SERS
substrate was monitored. The sensitivity of the Au@Ag-Au PPFs
SERS substrate preserved in air for the detection of BA decreased
slightly with increasing time (Figure 6F and Figure S13, Support-
ing Information). This was attributed to the replacement reduc-
tion reaction, leading to the transformation of the Ag shell into
an Au‒Ag alloy, which signiﬁcantly improves the stability. There-
fore, this SERS substrate can achieve stable SERS performance
without requiring special storage conditions. In addition, daily
diet plays an important role in the composition of the exhaled
gas. Common food items, such as rice, milk, and eggs, did not
seem to aﬀect the detection results (Figure S14, Supporting In-
formation).
We plotted the Raman intensity of the peak obtained at 1001
cm−1 versus the BA concentration, as shown in Figure S15 (Sup-
porting Information). The plot of the Raman intensity versus con-
centration was linear with a coeﬃcient of determination of 0.995
for BA concentrations ranging between 50 and 500 ppm and non-
linear for those between 0 and 100 ppm. Because the concentra-
tion levels of BA in the exhaled gas of cancer patients are gen-
erally between 10 and 100 ppb, this quantitative method based
on the Raman intensity‒concentration relationship is diﬃcult to
apply to the quantitative detection of trace BA. The diﬀerences
between the Raman spectra of diﬀerent BA concentrations are
not reﬂected from variations with respect to a single character-
istic peak only. Signiﬁcant diﬀerences are also observed in the
relative intensities and full widths at half maxima of the Raman
peaks. Therefore, we attempted to automatically extract complex
feature information from the high-dimensional spectral data us-
ing a CNN algorithm, which in turn established a relationship be-
tween the Raman intensity and concentration.[57,58] As the num-
ber of iterations increased, the accuracy rate tended to 1, and the

3. Conclusion
In conclusion, we designed and prepared an Au@Ag-Au PPFs
SERS substrate for the detection of gaseous BA. The structure
of the Au@Ag-Au PPFs is rich with localized electric ﬁeld dis-
tribution patterns, and the open framework structure allows for
eﬃcient transport of analytes, which improves the probability of
detecting low concentrations of molecules. The detection limit of
the Au@Ag-Au PPFs for the 4-MBA molecules was two orders
of magnitude lower than that of the traditional Au NCs. Selec-
tive detection of gaseous aldehyde biomarkers was achieved by
employing the L-Cys-modiﬁed Au@Ag-Au PPFs SERS substrate,
with weakened interference of other gases (ethanol, cyclohexane,
toluene, etc.). To match actual medical treatment, the modiﬁed
SERS chip was assembled to form a mask-type sensor, and its
working principle was investigated in detail. The automated and
accurate detection of the gaseous BA concentration was realized
from the detection results combined with the CNN algorithm.
The linear regression coeﬃcient between the predicted and ac-
tual results was 0.998. Therefore, this SERS sensor with excel-
lent sensitivity and speciﬁcity for aldehyde molecule analysis is
promising for providing a new perspective on the medical appli-
cations of SERS.
4. Experimental Section
Chemicals:
Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), cetyltrimethy-
lammonium chloride (CTAC), trisodium citrate, and pyrrolidone polyvinyl
(PVP) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich Co., Ltd. (USA), while sodium
borohydride (NaBH4) and ascorbic acid (AA) were obtained from
Acros Organics Co., Ltd. (Belgium). Silver nitrate (AgNO3), chloroau-
ric acid (HAuCl4), absolute ethanol (C2H5OH), methylene chloride or
dichloromethane (DCM, CH2Cl2), and n-Hexane (C6H14) were purchased
from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (China), while HCl, 4-MBA,
BA, EBA, acetone, ethanol (EtOH), n-butanol, n-pentanol, methanol, and
toluene were purchased from Innochem Reagent Co., Ltd. (China). All the
experimental reagents were used as received without further puriﬁcation.
Deionized water (resistivity = 18.2 MΩ·cm) was used for all experiments.
Synthesis of the Au Seeds:
Freshly prepared NaBH4 solution (100 mm,
0.06 mL) was rapidly added to a 10 mL solution of HAuCl4 (0.25 mm)
and CTAB (100 mm) under vigorous stirring for 2 min. The mixture was
kept undisturbed at 27 °C for 3 h. An aqueous solution of CTAC (200 mm,
4 mL), AA (100 mm, 3 mL), and the above solution (100 μL) was mixed
in a scintillation vial, followed by a one-shot injection of an aqueous. The
reaction was maintained at 27 °C for 15 min. The 10-nm Au seeds were
centrifuged at 15 500 rpm for 30 min.
Synthesis of the Au NSs:
An aqueous solution of CTAC (100 mm, 2 mL),
AA (10 mm, 130 μL), and the solution of 10-nm Au seeds (25 μL) was
mixed in a scintillation vial (20 mL), followed by the dropwise addition
of aqueous HAuCl4 solution (0.5 mm, 2 mL) using a syringe pump at an
injection rate of 2 mL h−1. The reaction was maintained at 27 °C for 10 min
after injection. The resulting sample comprised 40-nm Au NSs, which were
collected via centrifugation at 7500 rpm for 20 min.
Synthesis of the Au NCs:
The Au NCs were synthesized via a seed-
mediated growth method. An aqueous solution of CTAC (100 mm, 10 mL),
AA (10 mm, 65 μL), HAuCl4 (0.5 mm, 10 mL), KBr (100 Mm, 20 μL), and
the 10-nm Au NP solution (0.025 mL) was mixed in a scintillation vial (30
mL). The reaction temperature was maintained at 27 °C for 30 min. The
resulting sample comprised 40-nm Au NCs, which were collected via cen-
trifugation at 7500 rpm for 15 min.
Synthesis of the Au CNCs:
An aqueous solution of CTAC (100 mm,
10 mL), AA (10 mm, 100 μL), HAuCl4 (25 mm, 0.8 mL), HCl (1m, 200 μL),
AgNO3 (100 Mm, 20 μL), and the 10-nm Au seeds solution was mixed in a
scintillation vial (30 mL). The reaction temperature was maintained at 27
°C for 2 h. The resulting sample was centrifuged at 7500 rpm for 15 min.
Synthesis of the Au NCs@Ag NCs:
The solution of Au NCs (1 mL,
2.5 mm) was dispersed in the CTAC solution (10 mL, 20 mm) at 65 °C
under gentle stirring. Subsequently, 0.375 mL of AgNO3 (10 mm) and
1.87 mL AA (100 mm) were added. The mixture was maintained at 60
°C for 4 h, during which Ag was overgrown on the Au NCs to obtain the
Au NCs@Ag NCs. The resulting sample was centrifuged at 4500 rpm for
15 min. Au NSs@Ag NCs and Au CNCs@Ag NCs were prepared using
the same method.
Synthesis of Au NCs@Ag-Au PFs, Au NCs@Ag-Au DPFs, and Au
NCs@Ag-Au PPFs:
The solution of Au NCs@Ag NCs (1 mL, 1 mm) was
dispersed in a CTAC solution (4 mL, 50 mm) at 30 °C under gentle stir-
ring. Subsequently, 1 mL of NaOH (200 mm) and 1 mL of AA (100 mm)
were added to the above solution. Thereafter, 1 ml of HAuCl4 (0.5 mm)
was rapidly injected into the reaction solution and stirred for 15 min to
obtain Au NCs@Ag-Au PFs. Au NCs@Ag-Au DPFs and Au NCs@Ag-Au
PPFs were similarly prepared by varying the volume of HAuCl4 (1 and 2 mL,
respectively).
Synthesis of Au NSs@Ag-Au PPFs and Au CNCs@Ag-Au PPFs:
In the
above method, the Au NCs@Ag NCs were replaced with Au NSs@Ag
NCs and Au CNCs@Ag NCs to obtain Au NSs@Ag-Au PPFs and Au
CNCs@Ag-Au PPFs, respectively.
Self-Assembly of the NPs on Silicon Wafer or Filter Paper:
First, the
Au NPs were converted to PVP-coated NPs by two rounds of centrifuga-
tion and subsequently dispersed in ethanol for further use. Subsequently,
the PVP-coated NPs were mixed with 900 μL DCM in a 5 mL centrifuge
tube. Thereafter, 2 mL of deionized water was added to the centrifuge
tube under vigorous shaking for 10 s. Subsequently, 700 μL of n-hexane
was added along the wall of the container, and the NPs were driven
to the upper interface of the aqueous phase and n-hexane, thus form-
ing a closely packed NP monolayer. Finally, n-hexane was removed, and
the monolayer was transferred onto hydrophilic silicon wafers or a ﬁlter
paper.
Characterization and SERS Measurement:
The morphologies of the
NPs were characterized via SEM using an S-4800 instrument (Hitachi,
Japan). TEM images of the NPs were obtained using a TEM-2100 instru-
ment (JEOL, Japan). UV–vis absorption spectra were obtained using a
Lambda 750 spectrophotometer (Perkin Elmer, USA). A BWS415-785H Ra-
man spectrometer (B&W Tek, DE) was used to obtain the Raman spectra
of the samples at an excitation wavelength of 785 nm. The total laser en-
ergy was 300 mW, the laser power was 30%, and the integration time was
10 s for all experiments. Each spectrum represents the average value of
three SERS spectra.
Electric Field and Absorption Simulations:
To quantitatively interpret
the optical response of these structures, the commercial COMSOL Multi-
physics software was used to perform ﬁnite element method calculations.
The electric ﬁeld of the Au NPs arrays was determined using the FDTD So-
lutions software. To match the experimental conditions, simulation mod-
els were designed based on the SEM images of the substrates, and all the
simulation models had the same size as the actual object. The elemental
ratios of the Au and Ag nanoframes were determined from the elemental
mapping images. In the FDTD Solutions, a perfectly matched layer bound-
ary condition was applied for the x-, y-, and z-directions. The light source
used was a plane wave source with a wavelength of 785 nm, and the mesh
size was 0.5 nm for all the simulations.
